input.question: Why do storage devices such as hard drives, flash drives, and memory cards never have as much free space as the packaging says?
input.ground_truth: The SD card manufacturer measures data using standard metric measurements (1 GB = 10^9 B), while your computer uses binary versions of the measurement (1 GB = 2^30 B) since computers count in binary. So the computer's gigabyte (often listed as GiB to avoid confusion) is about 7% larger than the normal definition of a GB. Your flash drive still holds 32 billion bytes, but your computer reports those 32 billion bytes as 29GB and some change.

Okay! Imagine you buy a big box that says it can hold 100 toys inside. But when you start putting your toys in, you find out that some of the space is already taken up by the box’s own little pieces, like the cardboard dividers or the stickers on it. Also, sometimes the way the toys are packed (like how files are saved on a storage device) leaves tiny gaps that can’t be used.

So, when you see on the box, “holds 100 toys,” it’s counting the *most* it *could* hold if everything was perfect. But in real life, some space is used for the box itself or for helping the toys stay in place, so you have a little less space than the number says. That’s why your flash drive or memory card never has as much free space as the label promises!
